lessons.unit: Spring 2: Stone Age to Iron Age (Tribal Tales)
lessons.title: What was the Stone Age?
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we know about people who left no writing?
objectives: To understand how archaeologists use evidence to find out about the Stone Age
successCriteria: All: place the Stone Age at the start of a timeline
Most: say how hunter-gatherers found food
Some: explain what one artefact tells us
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: rocks such as flint (Year 3 Summer 2)
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at how Allah gave people skill to survive

keywords.def: the long time when people made tools from stone
a person who hunts animals and gathers plants for food
someone who digs up and studies things from the past
clues that tell us what happened
a hard stone that can be chipped to a sharp edge

hook.text: If someone dug up your bedroom in 5,000 years, what would they think about you?

islamicLink.text: Allah taught Adam the names of all things (Al-Baqarah 2:31). People have always been given minds to learn, make tools and care for the earth. History helps us see Allah's gifts to every generation.

starter.q: Which came first: the ancient Olympics or the World Cup?
BC dates are:
Name one material used to make tools today.

teach.heading: A very long time ago
bullets: Stone Age, Bronze Age, Iron Age
Each is named after a material for tools
teach.note: Build the timeline we will use all half term.

teach.heading: Hunter-gatherers
teach.note: They did not farm. They followed food.

teach.heading: Evidence
bullets: Remains of camps, like Star Carr in Yorkshire
teach.note: Archaeologists dig carefully, record where things are, and ask questions.

teach.heading: Reading an artefact
teach.note: Model with a flint hand axe.

model.problem: What does a flint hand axe tell us?
steps: Made of: flint, a hard stone
Used for: cutting meat, wood and skins
So: people hunted and made their own tools
model.answer: Stone Age people were skilled toolmakers who hunted

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: Hunter-gatherers got food by:
check.why: Farming came later, in the New Stone Age (Neolithic).

practice.q: What can animal bones at a camp tell us?
practice.a: What animals people hunted and ate
practice.model:
Find the clue: bones of deer.
Ask: why are they here?
Answer: people ate deer.
So they hunted deer.

practice.q: Why did hunter-gatherers move around?
practice.a: To follow animals and find plants in different seasons

practice.q: Which age comes after the Stone Age?

independent.q: Core: Look at three artefact photos (hand axe, antler tool, bone needle). For each, write what it was used for.
independent.a: Hand axe: cutting; antler tool: digging or a harpoon point; bone needle: sewing skins
independent.model: Teacher does the hand axe first using the three questions.

independent.q: Extend: Write one sentence: 'Archaeologists know ... because ...'
independent.a: For example: Archaeologists know people hunted because they found animal bones

independent.q: Stretch: What can evidence NOT tell us about Stone Age people?
independent.a: For example: their names, what they said, what they believed

exit.q: An archaeologist:
exit.a: Digs up and studies the past
options: Digs up and studies the past

exit.q: Big question: how can we know about people who left no writing?
exit.a: From evidence such as tools, bones and camps that archaeologists dig up and study

lessons.homework: Choose one object at home and write three things it would tell an archaeologist about you.
lessons.send: SEND: artefact cards with a word bank. EAL: tool, hunt, gather with pictures. Stretch: research Star Carr and what was found there.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Stone Age to Iron Age Britain
lessons.title: Hunter-gatherers of the Stone Age
objectives: Describe how Stone Age hunter-gatherers lived
Explain how stone tools were used

keywords.def: a person who finds food by hunting animals and collecting plants
a hard stone that can be chipped into a sharp edge
moving from place to place instead of staying in one home
paintings made on cave walls by early people

starter: Which comes first: Bronze Age or Iron Age?

teach.heading: Finding food
bullets: People hunted animals such as deer
They gathered nuts, berries and roots
They fished in rivers and seas
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and gratitude for food. Ask: where do we get our food from today? Compare with hunter-gatherers who had no shops.

teach.heading: Moving with the seasons
bullets: They lived in shelters or caves
teach.note: Explain nomadic simply: no permanent home. Britain was still joined to the rest of Europe by land for much of the early Stone Age, so people could walk here.

teach.heading: Stone tools
bullets: Flint was chipped to make sharp edges
Tools included axes, scrapers and spear points
Bone and antler were used too
teach.note: Show a picture of a flint hand axe. Ask what it might be used for: cutting meat, scraping hides, chopping wood. Do not claim pupils can try making real flint tools without safe supervision.

teach.heading: Art and fire
bullets: People painted animals on cave walls
Lascaux cave in France is famous
Fire gave warmth, light and cooked food
teach.note: Lascaux paintings are around 17,000 years old. Ask what the paintings tell us about what mattered to people. Avoid saying why they painted them as fact; historians are not certain.

practice: Name two ways Stone Age people found food.
Why did hunter-gatherers move from place to place?
independent: Draw a Stone Age camp (shelter, fire, flint tools, food) with labels
Write three sentences using the words nomadic, flint and hunter-gatherer
Choose: would you prefer to be a Stone Age hunter or a modern shopper? Give one reason
exit: Why were Stone Age people nomadic?
Which material was used to make sharp tools?
lessons.homework: List five foods you eat and say which of them a Stone Age person could have found without farming.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: picture word bank and sentence stems 'Stone Age people used ... to ...'. Stretch: explain one problem with finding food only by hunting and gathering.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Stone Age to Iron Age (Tribal Tales)
lessons.title: From hunting to farming: Skara Brae
lessons.bigQuestion: Why would people stop moving and settle in one place?
objectives: To understand how farming changed the way people lived in the New Stone Age
successCriteria: All: say what changed when people farmed
Most: describe a home at Skara Brae
Some: explain why farming led to villages
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: finding Orkney on the UK map
lessons.smsc: Social: how families and villages work together

keywords.def: growing crops and keeping animals
a place where people live together
the New Stone Age, when farming began
a Stone Age village on Orkney, Scotland
a stone shelf for keeping things

hook.text: Would you rather be a hunter-gatherer or a farmer? Why?

starter.q: Hunter-gatherers got food by:
A flint hand axe was used for:
Which age came after the Stone Age?

teach.heading: A big change
teach.note: The New Stone Age is called the Neolithic.

teach.heading: Skara Brae
teach.note: Show it on the UK map.

teach.heading: Inside a house
bullets: Stone beds and a stone dresser
A hearth fire in the middle
Roofs probably of turf or skins
teach.note: Stone furniture survived because there were few trees on Orkney.

model.problem: What does the stone dresser tell us?
steps: It is a set of stone shelves
It faces the door
People kept and showed things on it
model.answer: They had belongings and settled homes

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: Skara Brae is on:
check.why: Skara Brae is on Mainland, Orkney, off the north coast of Scotland.

practice.q: Why did farming mean people stayed in one place?
practice.a: They had to look after crops and animals
practice.model:
Crops take months to grow.
Someone must look after them.
So people stayed nearby.
They built homes and villages.

practice.q: What were Skara Brae's beds made of?
Why did stone furniture survive?
practice.a: Stone lasts; there was little wood on Orkney

independent.q: Core: Label the Skara Brae house plan: bed, dresser, hearth, door, passage.
independent.a: Five correct labels
independent.model: Teacher labels the hearth first: the fire in the middle.

independent.q: Extend: Write two ways a farmer's life was different from a hunter-gatherer's.
independent.a: For example: stayed in one place; grew wheat instead of gathering

independent.q: Stretch: What problems might farming bring?
independent.a: For example: bad harvests, animal disease, more work

exit.q: Neolithic means:
exit.a: The New Stone Age

exit.q: Big question: why would people settle in one place?
exit.a: To farm: crops and animals needed looking after, so they built homes and villages

lessons.homework: Make a model or drawing of a Skara Brae house with its stone furniture.
lessons.send: SEND: labelled photo to copy from. EAL: farm, crop, village with pictures. Stretch: compare Skara Brae homes with homes today.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Stone Age to Iron Age (Tribal Tales)
lessons.title: Stonehenge: a mystery from above
lessons.bigQuestion: Why would people drag huge stones for many miles?
objectives: To understand what we know and do not know about how and why Stonehenge was built
successCriteria: All: say one fact about Stonehenge
Most: describe Stonehenge from an aerial photo
Some: compare two theories about why it was built
lessons.smsc: Cultural: Britain's oldest monuments

keywords.def: a building or structure built to remember or mark something
a circle of huge stones in Wiltshire
seen from above
an idea that tries to explain something
a huge sandstone block

hook.text: How could people move a stone as heavy as a lorry without wheels or machines?

starter.q: Skara Brae is on:
Farming began in Britain in the:
Name one thing found inside a Skara Brae house.
starter.a: Stone bed, stone dresser or hearth

teach.heading: What is Stonehenge?
bullets: Built in stages from about 3000 BC
teach.note: Show it on the map of England.

teach.heading: The view from above
bullets: A circle inside a ditch and bank
teach.note: Aerial photos show shapes we cannot see from the ground. Use the aerial photo.

teach.heading: How was it built?
teach.note: No one wrote down how. Archaeologists test ideas.

teach.heading: Why was it built?
bullets: It lines up with midsummer sunrise
We do not know for certain
teach.note: Teach as history: what people may have believed then.

head: Theory
Evidence for it
rows: lines up with sunrise and sunset in summer and winter
many animal bones from feasts nearby

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: An aerial photo is taken:
check.why: Aerial means from the air, looking down.

practice.q: What does the aerial photo show that the ground photo does not?
practice.a: The circle shape, the ditch and the Avenue
practice.model:
On the ground I see tall stones.
From above I see a circle.
I also see a ring ditch round it.
So aerial photos show the whole shape.

practice.q: Where did the bluestones come from?
Do we know for certain why it was built?

independent.q: Core: Draw a simple plan of Stonehenge from the aerial photo and label the stone circle, ditch and Avenue.
independent.a: A plan with three labels
independent.model: Teacher draws the outer ditch circle first, then the stones inside.

independent.q: Extend: Choose one theory and give its evidence.
independent.a: For example: a calendar, because it lines up with the midsummer sunrise

independent.q: Stretch: Why can we never be sure?
independent.a: The builders left no writing, so we only have clues

exit.q: Stonehenge is in:
exit.a: Wiltshire

exit.q: Big question: why drag huge stones so far?
exit.a: It must have been very important to them, perhaps as a calendar, burial or meeting place; we do not know for certain

lessons.homework: Find Stonehenge on an online map in satellite view and draw what you see from above.
lessons.send: SEND: aerial photo with dotted outline to trace. EAL: above, circle, theory with pictures. Stretch: find the distance from Wales to Stonehenge on a map.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: The history of sports tournaments (Mighty Metals)
lessons.title: What is a tournament?
lessons.bigQuestion: Why have people always loved competing?
objectives: To understand what a tournament is and place famous tournaments on a timeline
successCriteria: All: say what a tournament is
Most: order four tournaments on a timeline
Some: use BC and AD to describe dates
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: ordering dates on a number line
lessons.smsc: Moral: good sportsmanship and self-control

keywords.def: a contest with many players or teams to find a winner
a line that shows events in time order
very, very long ago
the Middle Ages, about 1,000 to 500 years ago
years before and after the birth of Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him

hook.text: What is the best contest you have ever watched or played in? What made it exciting?

islamicLink.text: The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, held horse races (Sahih al-Bukhari) and encouraged archery (Sahih Muslim). He also taught that the strong person is not the one who wins a wrestling match, but the one who controls himself when angry (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). Sport in Islam builds the body and good character.

starter.q: Is 1969 in the past or the future?
Which is longer ago: 100 years or 1,000 years?
Name a sport played in teams.

teach.heading: What is a tournament?
teach.note: A football cup is a tournament. A single friendly match is not.

teach.heading: BC and AD
bullets: 776 BC is longer ago than AD 1066
teach.note: Draw a line with year 1 in the middle. BC counts backwards, AD forwards.

teach.heading: Tournaments through time
bullets: Modern Olympics and the World Cup
teach.note: Place each on the timeline.

timeline.label: 776 BC
timeline.text: First recorded ancient Olympic Games, Greece

teach.heading: Sport in Islam
bullets: Good manners when we win or lose
teach.note: Link to the Islamic foundation slide: strength with self-control.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: Which happened first?
check.why: 776 BC is the earliest. 1896 and 1930 are AD and much later.

practice.q: Order: 1930 World Cup, 776 BC Olympics, 1896 Olympics.
practice.model:
BC dates come first.
776 BC is first.
Then the smaller AD date: 1896.
Then 1930.

practice.q: Is a single friendly match a tournament?
practice.a: No: a tournament has many matches and one overall winner

practice.q: In which country was the first football World Cup?

independent.q: Core: Make a tournaments timeline with four events and dates.
independent.a: 776 BC ancient Olympics; 1100s jousting tournaments; 1896 modern Olympics; 1930 World Cup
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: draw a long line, mark year 1 in the middle, write 776 BC on the left.

independent.q: Extend: Add today's date and one tournament happening now.
independent.a: For example: a current football league or cup

independent.q: Stretch: How many years between the first modern Olympics and the first World Cup?

exit.q: A tournament has:
exit.a: Many matches and one overall winner
options: Many matches and one overall winner

exit.q: Big question: why have people always loved competing?
exit.a: For example: to test strength and skill, to have fun together and to win prizes

lessons.homework: Ask your family about a tournament they remember and add it to your timeline.
lessons.send: SEND: picture timeline cards to order. EAL: before, after, long ago. Stretch: find out when the first Olympic Games were held in London (1908).

lessons.unit: Spring 1: The history of sports tournaments (Mighty Metals)
lessons.title: The ancient Olympic Games
lessons.bigQuestion: What would an athlete at the ancient Olympics win, and why was that enough?
objectives: To understand what the ancient Olympic Games were like and how we know
successCriteria: All: say where and when the ancient Olympics began
Most: describe two events and the prize
Some: use evidence to say how we know about the games
lessons.smsc: Cultural: comparing an ancient culture with our own

keywords.def: the place in Greece where the games were held
Greece about 2,500 years ago
a running race of one length of the stadium
a ring of leaves worn on the head
things that show us what happened

hook.text: Would you train for years to win a crown of leaves? Why might it be worth it?

islamicLink.text: Islam encourages a strong, healthy body and fair competition. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said that a strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than a weak believer, while there is good in both (Sahih Muslim). The Greeks held their games for a false god; Muslims compete for good health and good character, for the sake of Allah.

starter.q: 776 BC is before or after year 1?
A tournament has many matches and one:
In which year were the first modern Olympics?

teach.heading: Olympia, Greece
bullets: Part of a Greek religious festival
teach.note: The Greeks held the games in honour of their god Zeus. We learn about this as history; Muslims worship Allah alone.

teach.heading: The events
bullets: Stadion: a sprint of about 190 m
teach.note: The pentathlon was running, long jump, discus, javelin and wrestling.

teach.heading: Who took part?
bullets: A truce let people travel safely
teach.note: A truce meant wars stopped so athletes and visitors could travel to Olympia.

teach.heading: The prize and the evidence
teach.note: Show the ruins of the stadium at Olympia. Pots and later writers tell us about the events.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: What did a winner at Olympia receive?
check.why: Medals came with the modern Olympics; ancient winners got an olive wreath.

practice.q: How often were the ancient games held?
practice.model:
Read the slide: held every four years.
So after 776 BC the next games were in 772 BC.

practice.q: Name two ancient Olympic events.
practice.a: For example: stadion sprint and wrestling

practice.q: Name one piece of evidence about the games.
practice.a: Ruins at Olympia, painted pots or old writings

independent.q: Core: Write a fact file about the ancient Olympics: where, when, events, prize. Use the portal response box or your book.
independent.a: Olympia in Greece; from 776 BC, every four years; stadion, wrestling, chariot racing; olive wreath
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: 'Where: Olympia, Greece. When: from 776 BC, every four years.'

independent.q: Extend: Give one way they were different from today's Olympics.
independent.a: For example: only Greek men could compete; the prize was a wreath, not a medal

independent.q: Stretch: If the games were every four years from 776 BC, when were the next two games?
independent.a: 772 BC and 768 BC

exit.q: The ancient Olympics were held in:
exit.a: Greece

exit.q: Big question: what would an athlete at the ancient Olympics win, and why was that enough?
exit.a: An olive wreath; the fame and honour back home were what mattered

lessons.homework: Make a top trumps card for one ancient Olympic event.
lessons.send: SEND: a fact file frame with picture prompts. EAL: race, prize, wreath, Greece. Stretch: research the Olympic truce.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: The history of sports tournaments (Mighty Metals)
lessons.title: Medieval tournaments: knights and archers
lessons.bigQuestion: Were medieval tournaments sport or practice for war?
objectives: To understand what tournaments were like in medieval England and why they were held
successCriteria: All: describe what a joust was
Most: say why kings wanted men to practise archery
Some: decide if tournaments were sport, training or both, with a reason
lessons.crossCurricular: English: writing a Point, Evidence, Explain paragraph
lessons.smsc: Moral: fair rules in competition

keywords.def: the Middle Ages, about 1,000 to 500 years ago
a soldier who fought on horseback
two knights on horses charging with lances
shooting arrows with a bow
a long wooden pole used by a knight

hook.text: If your country might go to war, why would you hold sports contests?

islamicLink.text: The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, recited the ayah 'prepare against them whatever strength you can' and said that strength is in shooting (archery) (Sahih Muslim). Muslims practised archery and horse riding as useful skills, with good manners and fair rules.

starter.q: Ancient Olympic winners got:
Where were the ancient Olympics held?
What does 'medieval' mean?

teach.heading: Knights' tournaments
bullets: Knights fought in teams at first
teach.note: Early tournaments were rough mock battles. Later, rules made them safer.

teach.heading: The joust
bullets: Points for breaking a lance on a shield
teach.note: Show a photo of armour and a lance in a museum (no people).

teach.heading: Archery contests
bullets: The longbow was England's great weapon
A law in 1363 told men to practise
teach.note: King Edward III ordered men to practise archery on holidays instead of other games. Archery 'butts' were mounds used as targets.

teach.heading: Sport or war?
teach.note: Let pupils argue both sides. The best answer: both.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: In a joust, knights:
options: Charged at each other on horses with lances
check.why: A joust was two mounted knights with lances, separated by a barrier.

practice.q: What did a knight use in a joust?
practice.a: A lance (and a horse, armour and a shield)
practice.model:
Look at the joust slide.
The long wooden pole is a lance.
So a knight used a lance.

practice.q: Why did kings want men to practise archery?
practice.a: So they would be skilled archers in war

practice.q: Name one way medieval tournaments were like sport today.
practice.a: Crowds watched, there were rules and prizes

independent.q: Core: Write a paragraph: Were medieval tournaments sport or training? Use Point, Evidence, Explain. Write in the portal response box or your book.
independent.a: For example: Point: they were both. Evidence: knights practised fighting and crowds watched for fun. Explain: so they trained for war and entertained people.
independent.model: Teacher shows it first. Point: Tournaments were training for war. Evidence: knights practised charging with lances. Explain: this made them ready for battle.

independent.q: Extend: Add a sentence about archery.
independent.a: For example: Men practised archery because the king needed archers for his army

independent.q: Stretch: How were medieval tournaments different from the ancient Olympics?
independent.a: For example: knights fought on horses; Olympic athletes ran and wrestled; prizes were different

exit.q: Archery means:
exit.a: Shooting arrows with a bow

exit.q: Big question: were medieval tournaments sport or practice for war?
exit.a: Both: they trained knights and archers for war and were also entertainment

lessons.homework: Design a shield for a medieval tournament using shapes and colours only (no people or animals).
lessons.send: SEND: a Point, Evidence, Explain frame with word bank. EAL: knight, horse, lance, bow, arrow with pictures. Stretch: find out what a 'butt' was in archery.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: The history of sports tournaments (Mighty Metals)
lessons.title: Modern tournaments: the Olympics, Paralympics and World Cup
lessons.bigQuestion: What has changed in tournaments since ancient times, and what has stayed the same?
objectives: To understand how modern tournaments began and how they compare with older ones
successCriteria: All: give the year of the first modern Olympics and first World Cup
Most: say what the Paralympic Games are
Some: give one change and one continuity
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: finding the difference between years
lessons.smsc: Social: respect and inclusion for disabled athletes

keywords.def: from recent times
games for athletes with disabilities
a football tournament between countries
something that is different now
something that has stayed the same

hook.text: Why do you think the Olympic Games were brought back after 1,500 years?

islamicLink.text: Islam teaches that every person has dignity and that Allah looks at our hearts and deeds, not our bodies (Sahih Muslim). The Paralympic Games show respect for athletes with disabilities, which fits this teaching.

starter.q: A joust used:
Ancient Olympics began in:
What prize did ancient Olympic winners get?

teach.heading: The Olympics return
teach.note: The Games came back in Greece to link with the ancient games.

teach.heading: The Paralympic Games
bullets: Began with games at Stoke Mandeville, England, in 1948
Now held after each summer Olympics
teach.note: Stoke Mandeville Hospital held games for injured soldiers; Dr Ludwig Guttmann started them.

teach.heading: The football World Cup
teach.note: Ask: why do you think so many people around the world love football?

teach.heading: Change and continuity
teach.note: Pupils add ideas in the chat.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Where was the first football World Cup?
check.why: Uruguay hosted and won in 1930. Greece hosted the first modern Olympics in 1896.

practice.q: How many years between 1896 and 1960?
What are the Paralympic Games?
Name one thing that has stayed the same since ancient times.
practice.a: For example: held every four years, or running races

independent.q: Core: Fill in a change and continuity table comparing the ancient and modern Olympics (3 changes, 2 continuities).
independent.a: Changes: medals not wreaths; women compete; athletes from all countries. Continuities: every four years; running races
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: 'Change: ancient winners got wreaths, now they get medals.'

independent.q: Extend: Add the Paralympics to your tournaments timeline.
independent.a: 1948 Stoke Mandeville games; 1960 first Paralympics in Rome

independent.q: Stretch: Why was starting the Paralympics an important change?
independent.a: It gave disabled athletes the chance to compete and be respected

exit.q: The first modern Olympics were in:
Big question: what has changed in tournaments since ancient times, and what has stayed the same?
exit.a: Changed: prizes, who can compete, many countries. Same: every four years, races, fame for winners

teach.heading: Londinium

teach.heading: Town life

Forts and small milecastles along it

check.q: Hadrian's Wall was built to:

practice.q: What did Londinium grow into?

Londinium was by the Thames.

keywords.def: a Roman town in the south of Italy
the volcano near Pompeii
the main square of a Roman town
a place where people live, bigger than a village
the stretch of sea next to Pompeii

hook.text: Would you live next to a big, quiet mountain with rich soil? What might you not know about it?

starter.q: The Romans invaded Britain in:
The Earth's outer layer is the:
Name one thing the Romans built.

teach.heading: Where was Pompeii?
bullets: At the foot of Mount Vesuvius
Close to the Bay of Naples
teach.note: Find Italy, then Naples, then Pompeii on the map.

teach.heading: A busy town
teach.note: Historians' estimates of the number of people differ. Stepping stones kept feet out of the dirt on the road.

teach.heading: The forum
teach.note: Every Roman town had a forum. Show a photo of Pompeii's forum with Vesuvius behind it.

teach.heading: Why live there?
bullets: The sea for trade and fish
Vesuvius had been quiet for centuries
teach.note: In AD 62 an earthquake damaged the town. People were still rebuilding it in AD 79.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: The main square of a Roman town was the:
check.why: The forum was the centre of town life.

practice.q: What was near Pompeii that would later destroy it?
practice.model:
I look at the map.
Pompeii is right next to a big mountain.
That mountain is the volcano Vesuvius.

practice.q: Give one reason people lived near Vesuvius.
practice.a: Rich soil, the sea for trade or fish

practice.q: What happened to Pompeii in AD 62?

independent.q: Core: Write a postcard from Pompeii in AD 78 describing the forum, a shop and the view of Vesuvius. Use the portal response box or the postcard sheet; start 'Dear friend, today in Pompeii I saw ...'.
independent.a: A postcard with three accurate details
independent.model: Teacher writes the first line: 'Dear friend, today in Pompeii I walked through the busy forum.'

independent.q: Extend: Label Pompeii, Naples, Vesuvius and the Bay of Naples on the map.
independent.a: All four labelled correctly

independent.q: Stretch: Why did nobody leave Pompeii after the earthquake of AD 62?
independent.a: They did not know Vesuvius was a volcano; it had been quiet for centuries

exit.q: Pompeii was in:
exit.a: Italy

exit.q: Before AD 79, most people thought Vesuvius was:
exit.a: A quiet mountain

exit.q: Big question: what could you learn from a town left as it was on one day?
exit.a: How people lived: their shops, food, homes and streets

lessons.unit: Summer 2: Pompeii (Tremors)
lessons.title: The eruption of Vesuvius, AD 79
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we know what happened at Pompeii nearly 2,000 years ago when there were no cameras?
objectives: To understand what happened when Vesuvius erupted and how we know about it
successCriteria: All: order the main events of the eruption
Most: explain how an eyewitness letter helps us
Some: say why the date of the eruption is debated
lessons.crossCurricular: English: writing a news report in time order
lessons.smsc: Moral: telling the truth about events and checking evidence

keywords.def: when a volcano bursts out lava, ash and gas
someone who saw an event happen
light rock full of holes, thrown out by a volcano
something that gives us information about the past
information that helps prove something

hook.text: If you saw something amazing happen, how would you make sure people 2,000 years from now knew about it?

starter.q: The opening a volcano erupts through is the:
Pompeii was damaged by an earthquake in:
What is the difference between magma and lava?
starter.a: Magma is underground; lava has come out

teach.heading: The eruption begins
bullets: A huge cloud rose from Vesuvius
Ash and pumice fell on Pompeii
teach.note: We teach this calmly. Many people left; some could not. We do not look at pictures of people.

teach.heading: Buried
bullets: Ash and pumice fell for many hours
Pompeii was buried about 4 to 6 metres deep
teach.note: Next, clouds of very hot gas and ash swept down the mountain and covered the town.

timeline.label: Day 1, midday
timeline.text: Cloud rises; ash and pumice fall

timeline.label: Day 2, morning
timeline.text: Hot ash clouds cover the town

teach.heading: An eyewitness: Pliny the Younger
bullets: He watched from across the bay
He later wrote two letters about it
He described a cloud shaped like a pine tree
teach.note: His letters were written to the historian Tacitus, years after the eruption. We paraphrase, not quote.

teach.heading: When did it happen?
bullets: A charcoal writing found in 2018 suggests October
teach.note: This shows how new evidence can change what we think.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: Pliny the Younger is useful because he was:
check.why: He saw the eruption himself, so his letters are a primary source.

practice.q: Put these in order: roofs collapse, cloud rises, town is buried.
practice.a: Cloud rises, roofs collapse, town is buried
practice.model:
First the volcano had to erupt, so the cloud rises.
Then ash piled on roofs until they collapsed.
Last, the town was buried.

practice.q: What fell on Pompeii first?
Why do some historians think it was October?
practice.a: Writing found in 2018 seems to date from mid-October

independent.q: Core: Write a news report on the eruption in the portal response box, with a headline, what happened in order, and what the eyewitness saw. Start: 'Vesuvius erupts! Yesterday ...'.
independent.a: A report in time order with ash and pumice, collapse, burial, and Pliny's pine-tree cloud
independent.model: Teacher writes the headline and first sentence: 'Vesuvius erupts! Yesterday at about midday a giant cloud rose from the mountain.'

independent.q: Extend: Is Pliny's letter a primary or secondary source? Why?
independent.a: Primary: he saw it himself

independent.q: Stretch: Give one reason Pliny's letters might not be completely accurate.
independent.a: He wrote them years later, from memory, and from across the bay

exit.q: Pompeii was buried by:
exit.a: Ash and pumice

exit.q: An eyewitness is someone who:
exit.a: Saw it happen

exit.q: Big question: how do we know what happened without cameras?
exit.a: From eyewitness letters like Pliny's and from what archaeologists find

keywords.def: someone who digs up and studies things from the past
dig carefully to find things
an object made by people long ago
a painting made on wet plaster on a wall
a picture made from tiny coloured tiles

hook.text: If an archaeologist dug up your kitchen in 2,000 years, what would they learn about you?

starter.q: Pompeii was buried by:
An earthquake is measured by a:
Who wrote letters about the eruption?

teach.heading: A lost town found
teach.note: The ash protected the town, so things survived that usually rot away.

teach.heading: Food and shops
bullets: A loaf of bread in a bakery oven
teach.note: The bread had turned to carbon in the heat, so its shape survived.

teach.heading: Words on walls
bullets: They tell us what people cared about
teach.note: Written sources from ordinary people are rare. Pompeii has hundreds.

teach.heading: Art and buildings
teach.note: Show the 'beware of the dog' mosaic: a dog, a tile picture at a doorway.

head: Find
What it tells us
rows: Homes were decorated; people had pets

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: Why did so much survive at Pompeii?
options: The ash covered and protected it
check.why: The ash sealed the town, so objects were protected.

practice.q: A carbonised loaf was found. What does it tell us?
practice.a: Romans baked bread in bakeries and ate it daily
practice.model:
I ask: what is the object?
A loaf in an oven at a bakery.
So it tells me people bought bread from bakeries, like today.

practice.q: What is an artefact?
practice.a: An object made by people long ago

practice.q: When did digging at Pompeii begin?

independent.q: Extend: Write a sentence: Pompeii is special evidence because ...
independent.a: Because the ash froze the town at one moment, so ordinary things survived

independent.q: Stretch: What can the finds NOT tell us?
independent.a: For example: what people thought or felt, or the exact date, without written sources

exit.q: Someone who digs up the past is an:

exit.q: A mosaic is made from:
exit.a: Tiny tiles

exit.q: Big question: why is the 2,000-year-old loaf so exciting?
exit.a: It shows us real Roman food and daily life, kept by the ash
